slides.title: Function
slides.say: A function is a named piece of code that a program can run whenever it needs that work done, from as many places as it likes. The textbook describes it as a mini program within a program (Sweigart, 2025), and the Python glossary states the same idea more formally: a series of statements which returns some value to a caller, and which can also be passed zero or more arguments that are used while its body runs (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The values passed in are called arguments, and the code that runs is called the body; both terms are defined carefully in the sections that follow. Without functions, every task that a program repeats would have to be written out again at each place that needs it, and a correction would have to be made in every copy. A function lets the programmer give the task a name, write it once and use the name from then on. The chapter adds a second reason: the variables created inside a function stay inside it, so a function can do its work and interact with the rest of the program only through the values it receives and the value it gives back, which narrows down the lines of code that can be responsible when something goes wrong (Sweigart, 2025). Functions are already familiar from chapter 1, where print, input and len were used as built-in functions that Python provides ready to use. This chapter shows how to write new ones with the def statement, how to call them, how to pass values in and get a value out, and what happens in the computer while one function waits for another to finish. Everything a Python program does beyond a few lines is organised into functions, whether the author wrote them or imported them from a module. The chapter is easiest to follow in the order of its own sections. Creating and calling a function comes first, then the two ways of passing values in (as parameters and as arguments), then the return value that comes out and the special value None. After that the call stack explains how Python finds its way back from a call, the scope rules explain which variable a name refers to inside and outside a function, and exception handling explains how a program can recover when a function fails. Two short animation programs and a note on current Python close the material. Two ideas that sound alike must be kept apart: the function itself, which is created once by a def statement, and a function call, which is each occasion on which that function runs. The practice questions of the chapter ask for exactly this difference (Sweigart, 2025), and most of the confusing error messages in the sections ahead come from mixing the two up. slides.title: Definition
slides.say: The definition branch covers how a function is created and how it is run. A function is created by a def statement, which names the function and gives it a body; it is run by a function call, which names the function again and supplies any arguments (Sweigart, 2025). Between the two lies a function object, the thing Python actually builds when it meets the def statement. Almost every misunderstanding about functions can be traced to the gap between defining and calling. A learner who keeps the two moments apart can predict when the code in a body runs, in what order a program prints its lines, and why a function must exist before the line that calls it executes. The sections of this branch go from the statement to the object to the call, and then to the reason for all of it. The def statement, the body, the function object and the keyword def come first, followed by the call, the call of a function that lives in a module, the lambda expression as a short way of writing a small function, and the function written inside another function. The branch ends with deduplication, the practical benefit that the textbook uses to justify functions. slides.title: Def statement
slides.say: Without def, a program could use only the functions that Python already provides. With it, the programmer names a piece of work once and every place that needs the work can use the name. The language reference calls a function definition an executable statement, which means that the function comes into existence at the moment the program reaches the def line and not before (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A def statement is found near the top of nearly every program that is longer than a few lines, usually above the code that calls the function. It can be typed in a file or in the interactive shell, and it can also appear inside the body of another function, which makes a nested function. When execution reaches a def statement, Python builds a function object and binds the function's name to it in the current namespace. It does not run the body; the reference states that the function definition does not execute the function body, which is executed only when the function is called (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program that defines hello with a print inside and then runs print('before') prints only the word before, because the greeting inside hello is never asked for. A function must be defined before the line that calls it runs. A program whose first line is hello() and which defines hello underneath stops with NameError: name 'hello' is not defined, because at that moment the def statement below has not been executed yet. The colon at the end of the def line and the indented body under it are both required, and the next section on the function body explains the error that follows when the body is missing. slides.title: Function body
slides.say: Python has no braces and no closing keyword to mark where a function stops, so the indentation is the only boundary. A line that is indented under the def line belongs to the function, and the first line that returns to the left margin belongs to the code that follows. Reading the indentation correctly is therefore the first step in reading any function. Every function has a body, and the body can contain any statement from the earlier chapters: calls to print, assignments, if statements with their elif and else parts, and loops. It can also contain a return statement, which ends the call, and further def statements, which create functions inside the function. The body is not executed when the function is defined. Each time the function is called, Python starts at the first line of the body and runs downward until it reaches the end of the block or a return statement, and then the execution continues on the line after the call (Sweigart, 2025). Variables that the body creates belong to that one call and disappear when it ends. A body must contain at least one statement; the statement pass does nothing and exists for the case in which a statement is required but no action is, such as a placeholder for a function that is still to be written (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A def line followed by no indented line, or by a line that is not indented, stops the program with IndentationError: expected an indented block after function definition on line 1. Equally easy to miss is a line that is indented by mistake: a statement meant to run once after the function but typed at the body's indentation becomes part of the body and runs only when the function is called.

slides.title: Function object
slides.say: Seeing a function as an object explains behaviour that would otherwise look arbitrary. The name can be copied to another name, passed to other functions, or reused for something else, because a function is a value like the numbers and strings of chapter 1. The reference makes the same point when it says that functions are first-class objects, which can be returned or passed around (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The object is visible whenever a function is named without being called. The call type(hello).__name__ gives 'function', callable(hello) gives True, and after same = hello the test same is hello is also True, because both names refer to one object. The same test works on a built-in function: callable(len) is also True. A built-in function such as len is reported as a built-in function or method instead, since it was not made by a def statement. The tutorial puts it plainly: a function definition associates the function name with the function object in the current symbol table, and other names can also point to that same function object and be used to access the function (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A function object also carries information about itself; its name is stored under the attribute __name__, an attribute being a named piece of information that is attached to an object and reached with a dot. Because the name is only a label, assigning to it replaces the function. After def hello(): and then hello = 5, the call hello() stops with TypeError: 'int' object is not callable. Writing the bare name hello with no parentheses does not call anything; it only refers to the object, so the line has no visible effect. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Reserved keyword
slides.say: A learner meets keywords as the words that start statements. Knowing that they are reserved explains an error message that would otherwise be puzzling: a program that tries to use def as a variable name, as in def = 3, stops with SyntaxError: invalid syntax, because the word already means something else. The textbook mentions keywords only to dismiss a confusion. It says that named parameters, which it also calls keyword arguments, have nothing to do with Python keywords (Sweigart, 2025). The word keyword in keyword argument means that the argument is given with the name of a parameter; the word keyword in def or return means a reserved word of the language. Whether a word is a keyword is a fixed fact about the language, and the keyword module can answer it. print is not on the list: keyword.iskeyword('print') is False, because print is a built-in function that can be given a new meaning, while def, return, global, nonlocal, try and except are all in keyword.kwlist and keyword.iskeyword('None') is True. The style guide adds that when a parameter name would clash with a keyword, a single trailing underscore is better than an abbreviation, so class_ is preferred to clss (Van Rossum et al., 2001). Do not confuse a keyword with a built-in name. A built-in name such as len can be reassigned by accident, which silently hides the function, whereas a keyword cannot be reassigned at all. The two situations produce different errors, and the section on the built-in scope returns to the first. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Lambda expression
slides.say: A def statement needs a name and several lines, which is more than a one-line calculation deserves when the function is used only once. A lambda expression can be written exactly where the function is needed. This course uses it mainly in examples, where it keeps a demonstration of parameters or return values to a single line that can be typed into the interactive shell. The expression (lambda a, b: a + b)(2, 3) evaluates to 5: the first pair of parentheses holds the function and the second pair calls it with two arguments. The language reference explains that the expression is shorthand for a simplified function definition and behaves like a def of a function named <lambda> whose body is a return statement (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The body of a lambda is one expression and nothing else. The reference states that functions created with lambda expressions cannot contain statements or annotations, so lambda: pass is rejected with SyntaxError (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The result is an ordinary function object, which has the name <lambda> instead of a name chosen by the programmer. The style guide advises against binding a lambda to a name with an assignment such as f = lambda x: 2*x and recommends a def statement, because the def form gives the function the name f instead of the generic <lambda> that appears in tracebacks and string representations (Van Rossum et al., 2001). In the program that assigns the lambda to add, add.__name__ is '<lambda>' while a def function called add2 reports 'add2'. slides.title: Nested function
slides.say: Nested functions let a helper stay next to the only code that needs it, without adding another name to the whole program. They also lead to the case of the scope rules that sits between a purely local and a purely global variable: a variable of the outer function, which the inner function can read and, with the nonlocal statement, can change. A small helper that is meaningful only inside one function is a typical nested function, and so is any function that builds and returns another function. Most beginner programs do not need them, but the nonlocal statement of this chapter and the lookup rule for names cannot be understood without them. Executing the outer function runs the inner def statement each time, so the inner function object is created anew on every call of the outer one. In the program that defines outer with a variable n set to 21 and an inner function that returns n * 2, calling outer() prints 42. Because the inner name is local to the outer function, using inner after outer has returned raises NameError: name 'inner' is not defined. Defining a function inside another one does not run it. The inner function runs only when it is called, and the outer function has to call it or hand it on. A nested function can read the variables of the outer function freely, but an assignment inside it creates a new local variable instead of changing the outer one, which is the reason the nonlocal statement exists.

slides.title: Function call
slides.say: A call is what makes a function do any work, because a definition alone runs nothing. It is also an expression: a call such as max(3, 7) evaluates to the value the function gives back, so it can be used wherever a value can, which later sections develop. Calls are the commonest construct in a program. The program in the textbook calls hello three times and prints ten lines, three greetings, the line ONE MORE TIME! and three greetings again (Sweigart, 2025). Calls to the functions of modules are written with the module's name and a dot in front, and the next section shows that form. The reference describes the order of events: every argument expression is evaluated before the call is attempted, and the thing being called must be a callable object, a function being the usual case (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Python then places the arguments into the parameters, runs the body, and returns to the line after the call when the body ends or a return statement is reached (Sweigart, 2025). The parentheses are what make it a call. A line that contains only hello does nothing visible, as the section on the function object shows. The number of arguments must also fit the definition: calling a function defined as hello() with one argument, as in hello('Alice'), stops with TypeError: hello() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Module function
slides.say: Most of the usefulness of Python lies in functions that other people have already written and placed in modules. The glossary notes that writing random.seed() makes it clear which module implements the function, and that the module's namespace prevents two functions with the same name from colliding (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The library documentation defines random.randint(a, b) as returning a random integer N such that a <= N <= b (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The call random.randint(5, 5) therefore always gives 5, and random.randint(1, 9) gives a number from 1 to 9 inclusive, which is how the fortune program picks one of its nine answers. The import statement of chapter 3 binds the module's name in the current namespace; the dotted name then looks up the function inside that module. Without the import line, the name random is simply undefined, and a program that calls random.randint(1, 6) first stops with NameError: name 'random' is not defined. Arguments given in the wrong order matter here, as they do everywhere. The textbook points out that random.randint(1, 10) is different from random.randint(10, 1): the first gives a random integer between 1 and 10 and the second causes an error (Sweigart, 2025). Running the second form under Python 3.12 and 3.14 raises ValueError in both, although the wording of its message differs between the two releases. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Deduplication
slides.say: Copies drift apart. If a bug is found in code that was pasted three times, the textbook warns, you must remember to change every place where you copied it. A function turns the three copies into one body and three short calls, so a correction is made once and is seen by every call. The chapter demonstrates the point with the greeting program. The version with a function has the three greetings written once and called three times; the pasted version spells out every print line, which makes it ten lines of print instead of four. Counting in the two sources, the text Good evening! occurs once in the function version and three times in the pasted version. The chapter's own pasted listing contains an example of the hazard it warns against. Its last line is print(' Good evening!') with a space before the G, so running the two programs gives outputs that differ in exactly that line: the function version prints Good evening! and the pasted version prints a line that begins with a space. Both outputs have ten lines, so the difference is easy to overlook, which is precisely the risk of duplicated code. A function is not the answer to every repetition. If the same few lines differ slightly each time, the differences should become parameters, which the next branch explains; if the repetition is a loop over the same steps, a loop from chapter 3 may be simpler than a function. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Parameters
slides.say: Parameters are the way values get into a function. A function definition lists the names that will receive the values, and each call supplies the values themselves. The textbook covers the plain form first, in the sections on arguments and parameters, and then the form in which an argument is identified by name, in the section on named parameters (Sweigart, 2025). A function that always did exactly the same thing would be of limited use. Parameters let one body serve many situations, such as greeting any person by name or dividing 42 by any number, so that the function stays short while the calls differ. They are also the controlled doorway through which a function receives information, because a function's own variables cannot be seen from outside. The branch begins with the vocabulary of define, call, pass, argument and parameter, then separates the two ways of matching an argument to a parameter, by position and by name. It continues with the two ways of forcing one of them, the slash that makes parameters positional-only and the star that makes them keyword-only, and ends with default values, which let a call omit an argument. The tutorial summarises the whole family in one definition line, def f(pos1, pos2, /, pos_or_kwd, *, kwd1, kwd2), where each marker restricts how the arguments that follow it may be passed (Python Software Foundation, 2026). slides.title: Parameter and argument
slides.say: The two words are used constantly in documentation, error messages and conversation, and they name two different things that are easy to swap. Using them correctly is what lets a learner read a sentence such as the third argument is not accepted by the second parameter without hesitation, and it is what the textbook means when it says that keeping these terms straight ensures that you know precisely what the text means (Sweigart, 2025). Every call in this chapter has both. The call say_hello_to('Alice') passes one argument, and the function prints three greetings that begin Good morning, Alice and end with Good evening, Alice; a second call with 'Bob' prints three more lines for Bob. The built-in call round(3.14159, 2) passes two arguments, the number and the digits to keep, and evaluates to 3.14. The textbook lists four verbs: to define a function is to create it, as an assignment statement like spam = 42 creates the spam variable, to call it is to send the execution to the top of its code, and to pass a value is to hand it to the function in the call. The arguments are then assigned to local variables called parameters (Sweigart, 2025). The reference adds that a function call always assigns values to all parameters mentioned in the parameter list, whether from positional arguments, from keyword arguments or from default values (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A parameter lives only as long as the call. The textbook points out that the value stored in a parameter is forgotten when the function returns, so print(name) after say_hello_to('Bob') stops with NameError: name 'name' is not defined (Sweigart, 2025). The number of arguments must also match the parameters: calling say_hello_to() with none stops with TypeError: say_hello_to() missing 1 required positional argument: 'name'. slides.title: Positional argument
slides.say: Position is the shortest way to write a call, and it is the form every function accepts unless its definition restricts it. It also means that the order of the arguments is part of the meaning of the call, so a learner who ignores the order will get wrong results or errors without any warning. The built-in divmod takes two numbers and returns a pair consisting of their quotient and remainder under integer division, which for integers is the same as (a // b, a % b) (Python Software Foundation, 2026); the two operators were introduced in chapter 1. divmod(7, 2) gives (3, 1), while the same two numbers in the other order, divmod(2, 7), give (0, 2), and divmod(17, 5) gives (3, 2). The textbook's own example is random.randint(1, 10), which is different from random.randint(10, 1) (Sweigart, 2025). The language reference describes the matching as a list of unfilled slots, one for each formal parameter: if there are N positional arguments, they are placed in the first N slots, and only then are keyword arguments assigned to slots by name (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A slot that receives two values raises TypeError, and a slot that is never filled and has no default value also raises TypeError. A positional argument may not follow a keyword argument in a call. The tutorial states that in a function call, keyword arguments must follow positional arguments (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and a call such as print('a', sep=',', 'b') is rejected before the program runs, with SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Named parameter
slides.say: Names make a call readable and let optional values be left out. The textbook says that programmers often use named parameters to provide optional arguments, and the clearest case is print: it has the optional parameters end and sep, which choose what is printed at the end of its output and between its arguments (Sweigart, 2025). A reader who sees end='' knows what it means without opening the documentation. Without any naming, print('Hello') followed by print('World') puts the two words on separate lines, because print adds a newline character at the end. With print('Hello', end='') the first call prints nothing at its end, so the output is HelloWorld on one line. The call print('cats', 'dogs', 'mice') prints cats dogs mice with spaces between the words, and adding sep=',' prints cats,dogs,mice. The coin-flip program of the textbook uses end=' ' so that the H and T results appear on one compact line, and two such calls followed by a bare print() give the line H T with a space after the T. The library reference defines print with the parameters sep, whose default is a single space, end, whose default is a newline, file and flush, and adds that sep, end, file and flush, if present, must be given as keyword arguments (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In an ordinary function, a parameter can be matched either way, so int('ff', base=16) and int('ff', 16) both give 255. When both a positional and a keyword argument try to fill the same parameter, as in f(0, a=0), the call stops with TypeError: f() got multiple values for argument 'a' (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A name that the function does not know is an error: print('a', separator=',') raises TypeError, and the wording of the message differs between Python 3.12 and 3.14. Because sep, end, file and flush are keyword-only in print, writing the separator as a plain extra argument does not set it; print('cats', 'dogs', ',') simply prints the comma as a third word, giving cats dogs , with spaces. slides.title: Positional-only parameter
slides.say: PEP 570 states the starting point: positional-only parameters have no externally usable name (Hastings et al., 2018). The tutorial's guidance lists the situations in which they fit: when parameter names have no real meaning, when the order of the arguments should be enforced, and, for an API (application programming interface, the set of functions that a library offers to other programs), to prevent breaking changes if the parameter's name is modified in the future (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Many built-in functions work this way. The call len(obj='abc') stops with TypeError: len() takes no keyword arguments, because the argument of len cannot be given by name. The reference notes that in CPython this is true of functions implemented in C that do not give their positional parameters names (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For a function defined as def f(a, /, b): return a * b, the call f(3, 4) and the call f(3, b=4) both give 12, because b may be passed either way. The call f(a=3, b=4) stops with TypeError: f() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments: 'a', which names the parameter that was misused. The worked example of this concept writes the same function as a lambda expression, which the section on lambda expressions explains. The slash separates parameters by how they may be passed, not by which ones are required. Everything before it is positional-only and everything after it, unless a star follows, can be passed either way. Introducing a slash into an existing function breaks any caller that used the name, so it is normally chosen when the function is first written. The worked example of this concept writes the same function as a lambda expression, which the section on lambda expressions explains. The slash separates parameters by how they may be passed, not by which ones are required. Everything before it is positional-only and everything after it, unless a star follows, can be passed either way. Introducing a slash into an existing function breaks any caller that used the name, so it is normally chosen when the function is first written. slides.title: Keyword-only parameter
slides.say: Requiring the name makes a call self-explanatory and removes a whole class of mistakes. The tutorial recommends keyword-only parameters when names have meaning and the function definition is more understandable by being explicit with names, or when users should be prevented from relying on the position of an argument (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The built-in print is the example learners meet first: its documentation states that sep, end, file and flush must be given as keyword arguments (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the textbook's examples this is why the separator and the end string are always written with their names. For a function defined as def f(a, *, b=2): return a + b, the call f(1, b=5) gives 6 and the call f(1) gives 3, because b has the default value 2. The call f(1, 5) stops with TypeError: f() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given, since the second value has no positional slot to fill. A star must come before the keyword-only parameters, and the keyword-only parameters are not required to have a default value: for def f(*, b), the call f(b=1) works and the call f() stops with TypeError: f() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'b'. The slash and the star can be combined in one definition, with positional-only parameters before the slash, keyword-only ones after the star and ordinary parameters between them (Python Software Foundation, 2026). slides.title: Default argument
slides.say: Defaults make the common case short and the unusual case possible. The call greet('Ada') returns Hello, Ada, greet('Ada', 'Hi') returns Hi, Ada and greet('Ada', greeting='Hey') returns Hey, Ada, so one function serves three styles of call. This is how the optional sep and end of print work. Defaults appear in the signatures of many library functions, and in the functions a program defines itself whenever a setting nearly always has the same value. The language also requires an order: if a parameter has a default value, all following parameters up to the star must also have one, and def bad(a=1, b) is rejected with SyntaxError: parameter without a default follows parameter with a default (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The default expression is evaluated once, when the def statement is executed, and the same value is then used for each call. The tutorial's example sets i = 5, defines def f(arg=i), then sets i = 6; calling f() still returns 5 and f(7) returns 7 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For the common values of chapter 1 this is invisible, but it matters when the default is a mutable object, an object that can be changed in place, such as a list. A list is an ordered collection of values that chapter 6 introduces. A default of def f(a, L=[]) that appends to L makes the one list be shared by all calls, so the calls f(1), f(2) and f(3) print [1], then [1, 2], then [1, 2, 3] (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The tutorial's remedy is a default of None that the function replaces with a new list when it is None, after which g(1) and g(2) print [1] and [2] separately. The test is written with is, which the section on identity explains. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Result
slides.say: The result of a function is what a call evaluates to once the body has finished. In everyday speech a function gives something back; in Python terms the call is replaced, inside the expression that contains it, by the function's return value. The textbook introduces the idea with a familiar case: when len is called with 'Hello', the call evaluates to the integer 5, and in general the value to which a function call evaluates is called the return value of the function (Sweigart, 2025). Parameters bring information into a function and the result carries information out. Together they make a function a small machine with inputs and an output, and this is what allows one function to be built on the results of another. A function that gives nothing back can still be useful for what it does, such as printing, but it cannot take part in a calculation. The branch has two parts. The first, about the return value, covers the return statement, the value that Python supplies when a function has no return statement, and the use of a call as an expression. The second, about the None value, covers the special value that stands for no value at all and the way to test for it. A function chooses its result with a return statement. If it never reaches one, Python supplies None. Either way the call can then be stored in a variable, printed, passed on as an argument or combined with operators, since a call evaluates to its return value. This divider is the branch's own description from the chapter corpus; the boxes under it name every concept in the branch, so the room can see how far there is to go.

slides.title: Return value
slides.say: The return value is the value that a function call evaluates to. It is produced by the function's return statement or, when there is none, by the value None that Python supplies. The three sections of this branch follow that order: the statement that chooses the value, the value supplied when no statement is written, and the use of the call itself as an expression. Understanding the return value separates two things that beginners often mix up, printing a result and returning it. A function that prints can only be read by a person, while a function that returns can be used by the rest of the program in arithmetic, comparisons and further calls. The reference puts the rule in one sentence: return leaves the current function call with the expression list, or None, as return value (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Everything else in the branch is a consequence of that sentence. slides.title: Return statement
slides.say: Without return, a function could only act on the outside world, for example by printing. With it, a function can compute something and hand it to the caller, which is how most of the functions in a real program are used. The textbook's fortune program is a typical case: get_answer receives a number and returns one of nine strings, and the main program prints the string it receives (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter's divide function is the simplest example. After def spam(divide_by): return 42 / divide_by, the calls spam(2), spam(12) and spam(1) evaluate to 21.0, 3.5 and 42.0, and spam(2) + spam(12) evaluates to 24.5, because the calls are values and can be added. In the fortune function, get_answer(1) returns 'It is certain' and get_answer(9) returns 'Very doubtful'. Executing return does two things at once: it computes the value and it leaves the function immediately. In a function whose first statement is return 'first' and whose second is print('never printed'), the call returns 'first' and nothing is printed, because the second statement is never reached. The program then continues at the line that made the call, and the call is replaced by the value. A return statement can appear several times, but only one of them is executed per call. In get_answer the nine return statements sit in an if and elif chain, and each call reaches exactly one; if no branch matches, as for get_answer(10), the function finishes without a return and the call evaluates to None. Any statement placed after a return in the same block can never run, as the print('never printed') example shows. slides.title: Implicit None
slides.say: Every call evaluates to a value, so every function must have some return value, and None is the choice that means nothing useful. It is the reason print can be used in an expression at all: the textbook explains that print displays text and does not need to return anything, but since all function calls need to evaluate to a return value, print returns None (Sweigart, 2025). The case appears whenever a function only performs an action, such as printing, and in every function whose last branch forgets to return. The tutorial's rule has two parts: a return without an expression argument returns None, and falling off the end of a function also returns None (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook also mentions that functions return None if you use a return statement without a value, that is, just the return keyword by itself (Sweigart, 2025). For def f(): pass and def g(): return the calls f() and g() both evaluate to None, and type(f()).__name__ gives 'NoneType'. The same is true of def add(a, b): a + b, which computes the sum and throws it away: add(2, 3) is None. The rule holds for built-in functions and methods too: [2, 1].sort() is None is True, because sorting a list in place hands nothing back. The interpreter normally suppresses None when it is the only value to be written, so in the interactive shell nothing appears after a call that returns it, but print(f()) writes it. A missing return is one of the most frequent mistakes in beginners' programs. The symptom is a calculation that seems to work but delivers None, followed by an error when None is added to a number or compared with one. When a function is supposed to give a value back, check that every path through it ends in a return. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Call as expression
slides.say: The principle behind the shortcut is the definition of an expression from chapter 1. The textbook reminds the reader that expressions consist of values and operators, and that you can use a function call in an expression because the call evaluates to its return value (Sweigart, 2025). A call is therefore just another value-producing piece of code, and it can be combined with every other one. Nested calls are read from the inside out. In len(str(42 / 2)), the division is evaluated first and gives 21.0, the call str turns it into the text '21.0', and len counts four characters, so the whole expression evaluates to 4. Calls also take part in arithmetic, as spam(2) + spam(12) does when it evaluates to 24.5. The language reference states the order: all argument expressions are evaluated before the call is attempted (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In print(get_answer(random.randint(1, 9))), Python first calls random.randint, passes its result to get_answer, passes that result to print and finally prints it. Each inner call has returned before the next outer call begins. Long nested calls are short to write but harder to debug, because no intermediate value is stored where it can be inspected. When a nested line does not behave, split it back into separate assignments as in the textbook's three-line version and print each stage. slides.title: NoneType
slides.say: NoneType is the data type of the single value None. The branch explains the value and the right way to test for it. Both points matter in this chapter because None is what every function returns when it has nothing else to give back. A language needs a way to say that there is no value, distinct from every real value including zero and the empty string. Python uses None for this, where other languages use null, nil or undefined, as the textbook mentions (Sweigart, 2025). The first section describes the value and where it comes from, with print as the standard example. The second section explains the test that decides whether a value is None, which uses the operator is instead of the equality sign. slides.title: None value
slides.say: None is useful when a variable has to hold something that shouldn't be confused for a real value (Sweigart, 2025). A function that searches for a result can return None to mean that nothing was found, a parameter can use it as a default to mean that the caller gave no argument, and a variable can start as None until its real value is known. The first place a learner meets it is the return value of print. After spam = print('Hello!'), the text Hello! is printed and spam holds None; printing spam then shows None, and the check None == spam gives True (Sweigart, 2025). The interpreter normally suppresses None when it would be the only value written, so a call to print typed into the interactive shell shows only its text (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The expression type(None).__name__ evaluates to 'NoneType', and the reference confirms that None is the sole instance of the NoneType type, that is, the only value of that type (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Because it is the only value of its type, any two Nones are the same object, which is the fact that the identity test of the next section relies on. None is also a keyword: keyword.iskeyword('None') is True, so a program that tries None = 3 stops with SyntaxError: cannot assign to None. None is not zero, not an empty string and not False, even though a test in an if statement treats all of them as false. The reference lists the values interpreted as false as False, None, numeric zero of all types and empty strings and containers (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The difference matters when a function must tell a missing value from a real zero, as the next section shows. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Identity test
slides.say: For None the identity test is the correct and the safest question. The style guide states that comparisons to singletons like None should always be done with is or is not, never the equality operators (Van Rossum et al., 2001). Since there is exactly one None, saying that a name is None is the same as saying that it refers to that one object. The textbook compares with equality, writing None == spam, which gives True and is not wrong in that example (Sweigart, 2025); the style guide asks that real programs use spam is None instead. The test appears in the default-argument pattern of this chapter, if L is None:, and in any function that must tell whether a caller supplied an argument. The same value can be tested in two ways, and only one of them asks the right question. A function describe(x) that answers 'missing' if x is None else 'given' reports 'given' for the argument 0, since 0 is a real value. A careless version written as 'missing' if not x else 'given' reports 'missing' for both 0 and None, because the reference counts numeric zero as false as well (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The style guide warns of exactly this trap: beware of writing if x when you really mean if x is not None (Van Rossum et al., 2001). It also asks for is not instead of not ... is, which is easier to read. Do not use is to compare numbers or strings: it tests identity, not equality, and Python even warns when it is written with a literal number. slides.title: Frames and the call stack
slides.say: A frame is the record that Python keeps for one running function call, and the call stack is the pile of such records that exist at a given moment. The language reference explains that a code block is executed in an execution frame, which contains some administrative information and determines where and how execution continues after the block's execution has completed (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter turns this machinery into a picture that a beginner can hold in mind. Every call has to return to the place that made it, and a function may be called from many different places. Python can only manage this if it remembers, for each call that is still running, where to go back to. The frames and the stack are how it remembers, and they also explain two things that look unrelated: why each call has its own variables, and why an endless chain of calls ends with an error instead of running forever. The textbook compares the call stack with a meandering conversation. You talk about Alice, are reminded of a story about Bob, and must first explain something about Carol; when the story about Carol ends you return to Bob and later to Alice. In a stack, items get added or removed from the top only, and the current topic is always at the top of the stack (Sweigart, 2025). The branch has one group, the call stack, with four sections. The first gives the order in which calls start and return, the second names the frame object that records each call, the third shows how a program can look at the frames it is running inside, and the fourth treats recursion, in which a function calls itself and the stack grows deep. The textbook itself says that the call stack is a technical detail that you don't strictly need to know about to write programs, and that it is enough to understand that function calls return to the line number they were called from (Sweigart, 2025). The reason to learn it anyway is that it makes the local and global scopes of the next branch easy to understand. This divider is the branch's own description from the chapter corpus; the boxes under it name every concept in the branch, so the room can see how far there is to go.

slides.title: Call stack
slides.say: The call stack is the stack of frames, one for each function call that has started and not yet returned. It is not a variable in the program; the textbook describes it as a section of your computer's memory that Python handles automatically behind the scenes (Sweigart, 2025). The stack explains the order of the output of any program with nested calls, and it is the reason an error deep inside one function can be traced back through the functions that led to it. Every concept in this branch is a view of the same stack: its order, its records, the way a program can inspect it and the way it can overflow. The sections of the branch take the stack in turn. They start with the order in which it grows and shrinks, continue with the frame object that is stored for each call, then show how to list the frames and how Python limits the depth, and finish with recursion. Use this slide to say what the next few slides are for before any of them appears: the table on the right is exactly the concepts that follow, each with the example the chapter uses for it. Click the rows in one at a time if the room is new to the material.

slides.title: Call stack order
slides.say: Without the stack, nested calls could not work. A function such as a() that calls b() must continue where it stopped once b() is done, and b() may in turn have called c() in the meantime. The stack keeps those waiting calls in the right order, with the function currently running at the top. The textbook's program abcdCallStack.py defines four functions: a() calls b() and then d(), and b() calls c(). Running it prints eight lines in this order: a() starts, b() starts, c() starts, c() returns, b() returns, d() starts, d() returns and a() returns (Sweigart, 2025). The nesting of the output is the nesting of the calls: c() finishes first, although a() started first. When the program calls a(), Python adds a frame for a at the top of the stack. The call to b() adds a frame above it, and the call to c() another one. When c() returns, its frame is removed from the top and execution continues in b() at the line after the call; the textbook stresses that frame objects always get added and removed from the top of the stack, and not from any other place (Sweigart, 2025). The top of the call stack is the currently executing function, and an empty call stack means that the execution is on a line outside all functions (Sweigart, 2025). A function that returns does not skip the functions that are waiting below it. Execution comes back to the immediate caller, never directly to the first one, which is why the lines c() returns, b() returns and a() returns appear in that order and not at once.

slides.title: Frame object
slides.say: Without a record of the caller, a function would have no way back. The frame is that record, and because each call gets its own frame, each call also gets its own set of local variables, which is how the same function can be running several times at once without the runs disturbing each other. A program can look at its own frames with the inspect module. In a function show defined as f = inspect.currentframe() followed by return f.f_lineno, f.f_back.f_lineno, the first number is the line currently being executed in that function and the second is the line of the caller; for the example program they are 9 and 10, the second being the line that contains the call x = show(). The documentation describes f_lineno as the current line number in Python source code and f_back as the next outer frame, the frame's caller (Python Software Foundation, 2026). When a function is called, Python creates a frame object on top of the call stack; when the call returns, it removes that frame object and moves the execution to the line number stored in it (Sweigart, 2025). The reference adds that a frame's f_back attribute points to the previous stack frame, towards the caller, or to None if this is the bottom stack frame (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the program in which inner() is called from outer(), the code name of the caller found through f_back is 'outer', and for a call made at the top level of the file it is '<module>'. Frames belong to Python's internals. The documentation of the inspect module warns that keeping references to frame objects can make the objects they reach live much longer than expected, and advises removing the reference once the work with the frame is done (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Ordinary programs never need to touch a frame; it is a tool for debuggers and for understanding.

slides.title: Stack inspection
slides.say: The stack is normally invisible, so being able to print it turns the textbook's picture into something a student can check. It is also how error reports are built: the lines of a traceback are the frames of the stack at the moment of the error, a point the exception section returns to. In a program where a() returns b(), b() returns c(), and c() returns the names of the frames from traceback.extract_stack(), the list is ['<module>', 'a', 'b', 'c']. The bottom entry is the top level of the file, then each waiting function, and the last name is the function that asked: c, the top of the stack. The interpreter also limits the depth of the stack. The documentation of sys.getrecursionlimit() calls the value the maximum depth of the Python interpreter stack and says that the limit prevents infinite recursion from causing an overflow of the C stack and crashing Python (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Under both Python 3.12 and 3.14 it is 1000, as the example evaluates. A stack that grows past the limit does not crash the program silently; Python raises RecursionError. The exceptions documentation says that it is derived from RuntimeError and is raised when the interpreter detects that the maximum recursion depth is exceeded (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Derived from means that RecursionError is a more specific kind of RuntimeError, so a program prepared for the general kind is prepared for the specific one as well; the exceptions branch calls this relation a subclass. The limit is a safety net and not a number to rely on: code that needs more than a few hundred nested calls is usually better written with a loop. slides.title: Recursion
slides.say: Some problems are naturally defined in terms of smaller versions of themselves. The factorial of 5 is 5 times the factorial of 4, which is a definition that translates directly into a function that calls itself with a smaller number. Recursion is also the clearest way to see the call stack at work, because the stack gets as deep as the chain of calls. For def factorial(n) that returns 1 when n <= 1 and otherwise returns n * factorial(n - 1), the call factorial(5) gives 120 and factorial(10) gives 3628800. Five frames for factorial exist at the deepest moment of factorial(5), and they are removed one after another as the results are multiplied on the way back. A recursive function needs a base case, a branch that returns without calling itself, so that the chain ends. The call stack holds one frame for each pending call, and each frame has its own value of n. When the deepest call returns 1, the frames below it are completed in reverse order, each multiplying its n by the value it receives. A recursive function without a base case never ends. For def forever(): return forever(), the stack grows until Python stops it with RecursionError and the message maximum recursion depth exceeded; RecursionError is a subclass of RuntimeError. A base case that is never reached because the argument does not shrink has the same effect as having none. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Scope
slides.say: A scope is the part of a program in which a name can be used, and the scope of a variable decides which variable a name refers to. The textbook asks the reader to think of a scope as a container for variables (Sweigart, 2025), and the language reference defines it as what determines the visibility of a name within a block (Python Software Foundation, 2026). This branch of the chapter explains the containers that exist, the rules that connect names with them, and the statements that bend the rules. Scopes are what keep a large program understandable. The textbook explains that Python uses scoping because it enables a function to modify its variables, yet interact with the rest of the program through its parameters and its return value only, which narrows down the number of lines of code that might be causing a bug (Sweigart, 2025). A bad value in a local variable can be hunted inside one function; a bad value in a variable that every part of the program can change could have been set from anywhere. Every program with a function has at least two scopes: the global scope that holds the names created outside all functions, and one local scope for each function call that is running. Beyond the textbook, a function defined inside another function has the outer function's scope around it, and every program can see the built-in names such as print and len. The branch starts with the containers, which the reference calls namespaces: the local scope, the global scope, the enclosing scope of a nested function and the built-in scope. It continues with the rules that decide which of them a name belongs to: the four rules of the textbook, the lookup order behind them, the statements global and nonlocal, the symbol table that applies the rules before the program runs, and two error messages, NameError and UnboundLocalError. The textbook allows global variables in small programs but calls it a bad habit to rely on them as programs get larger (Sweigart, 2025). The same habit is the main source of the surprising errors in this branch, because most of them happen when a function that reads a name is changed so that it also assigns it. slides.title: Namespaces
slides.say: A namespace is the place where a variable is stored. The glossary adds that namespaces are implemented as dictionaries, which are tables that pair a name with a value, and that there are the local, global and built-in namespaces as well as nested namespaces in objects (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A scope is the region of the program from which a namespace is visible, and in everyday speech the two words are used for the same container. Namespaces support modularity by preventing naming conflicts: the glossary's example is that the functions builtins.open and os.open() are distinguished by their namespaces (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The same idea lets two functions use the name eggs for different variables without disturbing each other. The sections of this group describe the namespaces one by one: the local scope that every call creates, the single global scope, the scope of an enclosing function, the built-in scope, and the confusing but legal situation in which the same name is used in several of them. Use this slide to say what the next few slides are for before any of them appears: the table on the right is exactly the concepts that follow, each with the example the chapter uses for it. Click the rows in one at a time if the room is new to the material.

slides.title: Local scope
slides.say: A local scope gives each call its own workspace. Because the workspace disappears afterwards, a function cannot leave clutter behind, and a variable called result in one function cannot be confused with a variable called result in another. This is the mechanism behind the textbook's image of a function as a black box. In the program that defines spam with the line eggs = 'sss' and calls spam(), the variable eggs exists only while spam runs. The textbook explains that a new local scope gets created whenever a program calls a function, and that when the function returns the local scope gets destroyed, along with these variables (Sweigart, 2025). The destruction has a visible effect. After the call, print(eggs) at the top level stops with NameError: name 'eggs' is not defined, because there is no variable of that name any more. A function that sets n = 0 and adds one to it always starts fresh: calling counter() twice gives 1 and 1, not 1 and 2, since the second call receives a new local scope in which n starts again. Values that must survive from one call to the next cannot live in a local variable. They can be returned to the caller, which stores them, or they can live in a global variable, which brings the risks that the global scope section describes. The parameters of a function also belong to its local scope and are forgotten at the return.

slides.title: Global scope
slides.say: A global variable is the simplest way for different functions to share a value, which is why beginners reach for it first. It is also the reason the textbook recommends caution: when every function can change a variable, a bug caused by a bad value gives no hint about where the value was set. The program that sets eggs = 'GLOBALGLOBAL' at the top level and then calls a function that prints eggs shows the usual use: the function does not assign the name, so it reads the global one and prints GLOBALGLOBAL. There is only one global scope. It is created when the program begins and destroyed when the program terminates, at which time all its variables are forgotten, whereas a new local scope is created for every call (Sweigart, 2025). Code in a function can read a global variable freely; changing it needs the global statement that a later section describes. The global scope is not the same as the built-in scope. A name such as print is found in neither the local nor the global scope of the program, and yet it works, because the built-in scope is searched last. Mixing the two up leads to the mistake of redefining a built-in name as a global variable.

slides.title: Same-name variables
slides.say: The rule is what makes functions independent. A programmer writing spam does not need to know whether bacon already uses the name eggs. The cost is that a reader can be confused about which eggs is meant at a given line, which the FAQ describes by saying that an assignment to a variable in a scope makes it local to that scope and shadows any similarly named variable in the outer scope (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook's program localGlobalSameName.py defines spam with its own eggs set to 'spam local', and bacon with another eggs set to 'bacon local' that calls spam and prints its own eggs again; at the top level eggs is 'global'. Calling bacon() and then printing eggs gives four lines: bacon local, spam local, bacon local and global (Sweigart, 2025). The program contains three different variables that are all named eggs: one in the local scope of spam, one in the local scope of bacon, and one in the global scope (Sweigart, 2025). While spam runs, the eggs of bacon still exists, waiting on the call stack, and it has not been changed. When bacon prints eggs for the second time it still shows its own value. Legal does not mean advisable. The textbook's advice is that, to simplify your life, you should avoid using the same name in different scopes and give all variables unique names, even when they appear in different scopes (Sweigart, 2025). In practice, this means that a function should not reuse the name of a global variable for something else. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Enclosing scope
slides.say: The enclosing scope completes the picture of where a name can be found. A name used inside a nested function is searched in its own local scope first, then in the enclosing scopes from the nearest to the farthest, then in the global scope, and finally in the built-in scope, as the tutorial describes (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the program in which outer sets n = 21 and defines an inner function that returns n * 2, the call outer() evaluates to 42: the inner function has no n of its own and finds the one in outer. The worked example of this concept builds the same structure from two lambda expressions and evaluates to 42. The glossary notes that nested scopes by default work only for reference and not for assignment: local variables both read and write in the innermost scope, and the nonlocal statement allows writing to outer scopes (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In other words, an inner function reads the variables of its enclosing function freely, but an assignment inside it creates a new local variable. A name read from an enclosing scope is looked up when the inner function runs, not when it is defined. If the outer variable changes in between, the inner function sees the new value. The FAQ shows the surprising consequence for functions created in a loop, which all see the final value of the loop variable (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Built-in scope
slides.say: This is why print works without any definition and without an import, even though the program never created that name. It is also why the FAQ can say that if global were required for all global references, you would have to declare as global every reference to a built-in function or to a component of an imported module (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The tutorial puts the built-ins at the end of the lookup order: variable references first look in the local symbol table, then in the local symbol tables of enclosing functions, then in the global symbol table, and finally in the table of built-in names (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The check builtins.len is len evaluates to True, which shows that the len that a program sees is the one in the builtins module. A function such as reads_len that returns len('abc') finds len in none of the scopes it owns, so the search ends in the built-in scope and the call evaluates to 3. A name assigned in a nearer scope hides the built-in one: inside a function, len = 3 makes len a local variable that equals 3, and the real len is untouched for the rest of the program. Hiding a built-in name at the top level breaks every later use of it. After len = 3 at the top level of a program, the call len('abc') stops with TypeError: 'int' object is not callable, since the name now refers to the number 3. Avoid using built-in names such as len, print, max or type for variables. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Scope rules
slides.say: The scope rules are the statements that decide whether a name in a function is local or global, and what happens when a program breaks them. The textbook states two sets of rules: four rules that say what code can use which variables, and four rules for identifying whether a variable belongs to a local or the global scope (Sweigart, 2025). Following the rules is the difference between a program that works and one that stops with an error that looks arbitrary. The rules also explain a surprising fact: whether a name is local is decided from the text of the whole function, not from the line that is running. The sections cover what code can reach which scope, the lookup order behind it, the two statements that change the rules, the table in which the compiler, the part of Python that translates the program into bytecode, records its decisions, and the two errors that appear when a name cannot be found. A last section covers the statement nonlocal, which the textbook omits. Use this slide to say what the next few slides are for before any of them appears: the table on the right is exactly the concepts that follow, each with the example the chapter uses for it. Click the rows in one at a time if the room is new to the material.

slides.title: Local isolation
slides.say: Isolation is what makes a function a black box. A function can be rewritten, renamed or have its variables changed without affecting any other part of the program, because no other part can see them. In the first case a function spam assigns eggs = 'sss', and the line print(eggs) after the call stops with NameError: name 'eggs' is not defined. In the second case spam sets eggs to 'SPAMSPAM' and calls bacon, which sets its own eggs to 'BACONBACON' and a variable ham; back in spam, print(eggs) shows SPAMSPAM, because bacon's variables are in another scope (Sweigart, 2025). Python creates a new local scope whenever a program calls a function, even when the function is called from another function, and multiple local scopes can exist at the same time (Sweigart, 2025). The variable ham of bacon exists only during that call. If a third function tries to print ham, it stops with NameError: name 'ham' is not defined. The only legitimate ways to move information between functions are the parameters and the return value. A learner who wants to read another function's variable should return it from that function, or pass it as an argument, and not reach for a global.

slides.title: Global access
slides.say: Without this rule every function would need to be handed every constant, setting and helper function as a parameter. The FAQ gives the reason that the default is the way it is: if global were required for all global references, you'd be using global all the time (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the program where eggs = 'GLOBALGLOBAL' is assigned at the top level and spam only prints eggs, the call spam() prints GLOBALGLOBAL. The practice questions of the chapter use the same rule: a program assigns random_number = random.randint(1, 6) once at the top level and defines a function that only returns random_number (Sweigart, 2025). That function returns the same number on every call, because the random choice was made once, when the global variable was assigned, and the function only reads it. Counting the different values among four calls gives 1. Calling randint inside the function would have chosen a new number each time. Reading a global is allowed, but the first assignment inside the function changes the meaning of every use in that function. The FAQ states the rule briefly: variables that are only referenced inside a function are implicitly global, and if a variable is assigned a value anywhere within the function's body, it's assumed to be a local unless explicitly declared as global (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

slides.title: Name resolution
slides.say: A single rule is easier to remember and to apply than a list of exceptions. Once the order is known, every scope question can be answered by walking through the scopes from the nearest outward and stopping at the first one that has the name. The tutorial gives the order: first the local symbol table, then the symbol tables of enclosing functions, then the global symbol table, and finally the table of built-in names (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the program with a global x set to 'global', an outer function that sets x = 'enclosing', and an inner function that only returns x, the inner function returns 'enclosing', a second inner function that assigns x = 'local' returns 'local', and the global x is still 'global'. The search finds the name in the nearest scope that has it and stops there. If the name is not found in any scope, the reference says that a NameError exception is raised (Python Software Foundation, 2026). If the name was bound in the current function but not yet given a value at the moment of use, an UnboundLocalError is raised instead, which is the subject of a later section. Resolution depends on the structure of the program text, not on the order in which lines happen to run. A name is resolved in the local scope if the function assigns it anywhere, even in a branch that never executes, and then it is a local variable for the whole function, as the section on the symbol table shows.

slides.title: NameError
slides.say: It is the commonest error in beginners' programs and the one that the scope rules most directly explain. Reading the message correctly, a learner can tell at once whether the name was misspelled, used before it was created, or created in a scope that the line cannot see. The chapter shows it in the first scope rule: print(eggs) at the top level, after a function has assigned eggs locally, gives NameError: name 'eggs' is not defined. A misspelled or differently capitalised name behaves the same way, since Python distinguishes capitals: after def Hello(), the call hello() reports that the name hello is not defined, and recent releases add the hint Did you mean: 'Hello'? The reference says that when a name is not found at all, a NameError exception is raised (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Several of the situations in this chapter reach it by different roads: a call before the def statement has run, a variable that exists only in another function, a parameter used after its call has returned, and a function name that is only defined inside another function. UnboundLocalError is a subclass of NameError, so an except clause for NameError also catches it. The two should not be confused when reading a message: NameError says there is no such name at all, while UnboundLocalError says that the name exists in the function but has no value yet.

slides.title: Global statement
slides.say: Reading a global needs no declaration, but changing one does: the reference notes that it would be impossible to assign to a global variable without global (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The requirement is deliberate, since the FAQ says that requiring global for assigned variables provides a bar against unintended side-effects (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the textbook's globalStatement.py, the function spam declares global eggs and then assigns eggs = 'spam'. After the top-level eggs was set to 'global', calling spam() and printing eggs gives spam, because no local eggs is ever created (Sweigart, 2025). The statement applies to the entire current scope, and a SyntaxError is raised if the variable is used or assigned to before its global declaration in that scope (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A function that assigns eggs = 1 and only afterwards declares global eggs is rejected with SyntaxError: name 'eggs' is assigned to before global declaration, before the program runs. Needing global is a hint that the design may be wrong. The textbook says that writing functions without global variables is encouraged, which makes it possible to treat each function as a black box (Sweigart, 2025). Pass values in as parameters and take results out as return values, and keep the global statement for the few cases that truly need it. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Scope identification
slides.say: The four rules turn the earlier discussion into a procedure that a student can carry out on paper. Looking at a function, one finds first any global statement, then any assignment, and the name is classified accordingly. The rules also fit into the one lookup rule of the previous section. The textbook's sameNameLocalGlobal.py has three functions that use the name eggs. In spam, which declares global eggs, it is the global variable; in bacon, which assigns eggs = 'bacon', it is local; and in ham, which only prints eggs, it is the global variable (Sweigart, 2025). Running spam(), printing eggs, then running bacon() and printing eggs, then ham() prints spam three times, because only spam changes the global. The decision does not depend on the order of the lines. The reference explains that the local variables of a code block can be determined by scanning the entire text of the block for name binding operations (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and the symbol table of the next but one section shows the result: the same name eggs is global in spam, local in bacon and global in ham. Rule 4 has a trap that rule 3 creates: a function that only uses a name is reading the global one, but adding one assignment anywhere in the function turns every use of that name in it into the local variable. This is the origin of the error described in the section on UnboundLocalError.

slides.title: Symbol table
slides.say: The table explains why the scope rules look at the text of a function and not at what is executed. Python decides which names are local before the first line of the function runs, so no behaviour at run time can change the decision. The module symtable lets a program read the compiler's decisions. For a source with spam declaring global eggs, bacon assigning eggs and ham only printing it, the table lists eggs as global for spam, local for bacon and global for ham, which agrees with the textbook's four rules. The decision is made for the whole function body at once. In a function that contains if False: followed by an indented assignment x = 'local', and then returns x, the assignment never runs, and yet x is a local variable of the function, so the call stops with UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'x' where it is not associated with a value. The global x that was set earlier is not used. The symbol table is an inspection tool and not part of normal programming. Its structure can change between releases: in Python 3.14 every function in this example also has a separate block for its annotations, which the example filters out by name.
