slides.title: UnboundLocalError
slides.say: The error is confusing because the name does exist in the program: a global variable of the same name was perhaps assigned earlier. It appears exactly when the rule of scope identification and the order of the lines disagree, and understanding it is the best test of whether a learner has understood how Python classifies names. The textbook's sameNameError.py prints eggs on its first line and assigns eggs = 'spam local' on its second, while a global eggs exists. Python sees the assignment and therefore considers any mention of eggs in spam to be a local variable; because print(eggs) runs first, the local variable does not exist yet, and Python won't fall back to using the global eggs (Sweigart, 2025). The FAQ gives a second form of the same mistake: with a global x = 10, a function that prints x and then executes x += 1 fails, because the assignment x += 1 makes x local (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Declaring global x repairs it when the global is meant, as does a nonlocal declaration for the variable of an enclosing function; renaming the local variable repairs it when it is not. The wording of the message has changed. The textbook prints local variable 'eggs' referenced before assignment, which is what Python 3.10 prints for the program, but Python 3.11 and every later release, including 3.12 and 3.14, print cannot access local variable 'eggs' where it is not associated with a value. The kind of error, which Python calls its class, and the cause are the same, so a program must match the class and never the message. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Nonlocal statement
slides.say: It completes the set of choices for where an assignment goes. An assignment inside a function normally creates a local variable, global makes it go to the module's variable, and nonlocal makes it go to the nearest enclosing function's variable. PEP 3104 gives the historical reason: before it, Python code could refer to a name in any enclosing scope, but could only rebind names in two scopes, the local scope and the module-global scope (Yee, 2006). In outer, set n = 0 and define inner with the line nonlocal n and the statement n += 1. After outer calls inner twice and returns n, it returns 2. Without the nonlocal line, the statement n += 1 would make n a local variable of inner, which has no value yet, and the call stops with UnboundLocalError. If a name is bound in more than one nonlocal scope, the nearest binding is used (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The statement applies to the entire scope of the function and must come before any use of the name there. If the name is not bound in any enclosing function, the program is rejected before it runs with SyntaxError: no binding for nonlocal 'q' found. Do not use nonlocal when a return value would do. Like global, it makes a function depend on state outside itself, and a reader has to look at the enclosing function to understand it. It is useful mainly for small helper functions that keep a counter or a running total for their enclosing function. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Error handling
slides.say: Error handling is the part of a program that decides what happens when something goes wrong. In Python an error that stops a statement is called an exception, and the language has two statements for dealing with it: try marks the code that might fail, and except says what to do when it does. The textbook puts the problem plainly: right now, getting an error, or exception, in a Python program means the entire program will crash (Sweigart, 2025). A program that crashes on the first unexpected input cannot be used for real work. The textbook says that in real-world programs you want the program to detect errors, handle them, and then continue to run (Sweigart, 2025), and its chapter summary adds that the try and except statements make programs more resilient to common error cases. A program that handles an error can also give a useful message, such as asking the user to type a number again, where an unhandled error shows a traceback that only a programmer can read. The branch has one group, Exceptions. It begins with the try and except statements themselves, follows an error out of a function into the code that called it, and covers the newest change to the except line. It then looks at the objects that carry an error, the report Python prints when nobody handles one, the divide-by-zero error that the chapter uses as its example, and the family tree that decides which except clause catches which error. When a statement raises an exception, Python stops running the block it is in and looks for a handler: an except clause, on a try statement, that names a matching exception. If one is found its block runs and the program continues after the try statement. If none is found anywhere in the chain of calls, the program ends with a traceback (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The textbook points out that most of the time exceptions indicate a bug in your code that you need to fix (Sweigart, 2025). Handling an error is the right tool for failures that can be expected and recovered from, such as a missing file or text that is not a number, and the wrong tool for hiding a mistake in the program itself. This divider is the branch's own description from the chapter corpus; the boxes under it name every concept in the branch, so the room can see how far there is to go.

slides.title: Exceptions
slides.say: An exception is Python's way of reporting that a statement could not be carried out. The tutorial separates two kinds of mistake: syntax errors, also known as parsing errors, and errors detected during execution, which are called exceptions and are not unconditionally fatal (Python Software Foundation, 2026). This group is about the second kind, and about the statements that let a program survive them. The tutorial notes that most exceptions are not handled by programs, however, and result in error messages (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Knowing how an exception travels, what it carries and which handler catches it turns those messages from a source of panic into a description of what happened, and lets a program choose to recover when recovery makes sense. The sections follow the life of one exception: the statements that catch it, the way it leaves a function, the spelling for catching several kinds at once, the object that Python creates for it, the report printed when it is not caught, the arithmetic error used as the chapter's example, and the hierarchy of classes that organises all of them. Use this slide to say what the next few slides are for before any of them appears: the table on the right is exactly the concepts that follow, each with the example the chapter uses for it. Click the rows in one at a time if the room is new to the material.

slides.title: Try and except
slides.say: Without a handler, the first error ends the program. With one, the program can report a problem in its own words and go on with its work. The textbook motivates this with a later chapter, in which a missing file raises FileNotFoundError and the program may ask the user for the filename again rather than crash (Sweigart, 2025). The textbook puts the divide-by-zero code of its function spam inside a try clause, with the line except ZeroDivisionError: below it. Called with 2, 12, 0 and 1, the program prints 21.0, then 3.5, then Error: Invalid argument., then None, then 42.0. The None comes from the third call, because the handler prints a message but the function then ends without a return statement and supplies None, which print shows. The tutorial gives the rules. First the try clause is executed. If no exception occurs the except clause is skipped. If an exception occurs, the rest of the try clause is skipped, and if its type matches the exception named after the except keyword, the except clause is executed and execution continues after the try and except block. If the type does not match, the exception is passed on to outer try statements, and if no handler is found, it is an unhandled exception and execution stops with an error message (Python Software Foundation, 2026). An exception that does not match is not swallowed. When spam is called with the text 'a' instead of a number, the division raises a TypeError, which the clause for ZeroDivisionError does not match, and the program ends with the message unsupported operand type(s) for /: 'int' and 'str'. The tutorial adds that a handler only handles exceptions that occur in the corresponding try clause, not in other handlers of the same try statement (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Error in a called function
slides.say: This lets one handler protect many calls, and it keeps the error handling in the place where the program knows what to do about the error. A function such as spam can stay short and simply fail; the code that called it decides whether failure means a message, a second attempt or a clean exit. In the textbook's second version of the divide-by-zero program, spam only divides, and the four print(spam(...)) lines are inside the try clause. The output is 21.0, then 3.5, then Error: Invalid argument. The fourth call, print(spam(1)), is never executed. The textbook explains why: once the execution jumps to the code in the except clause, it does not return to the try clause, but continues moving down the program as normal (Sweigart, 2025). The error leaves spam and passes to the code that called it. The traceback of the unhandled version shows the two frames the error passed through, the line in the main program that called spam and the line inside spam that divided; the handler of the second version belongs to the first of them, the main program. Where the try statement is placed decides how much code is skipped. With the try inside spam, as in the first version, the failing call returns None and the program goes on to the fourth call, so 42.0 is printed. With the try around all four calls, the program skips the fourth call as well. Neither placement is wrong; they answer different questions, which are whether each call is allowed to fail alone and whether the first failure ends the whole group of calls. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Several exception types in one except
slides.say: The change comes from PEP 758, whose abstract says that it allows unparenthesized except and except* blocks only when not using the as clause. Its authors call the brackets a Python 2 remnant and argue that dropping them makes the syntax more consistent with other parts of the language where parentheses are optional (Galindo Salgado and Cannon, 2024). Take a function that divides 10 by int(x) and should answer bad for both a zero and a text that is not a number. The call with '2' gives 5.0, and the calls with '0' and 'puppy' each give bad. With the names in brackets the function works in Python 3.12 and 3.14. Written as except ZeroDivisionError, ValueError: it gives the same results in Python 3.14, while Python 3.12 refuses to run the program and reports SyntaxError: multiple exception types must be parenthesized. The semantics are unchanged: the interpreter will catch any of the listed exceptions, whether or not they are in brackets (Galindo Salgado and Cannon, 2024). A separate except clause for each type is the other choice, and it is the right one when the types need different responses. With one clause for ZeroDivisionError returning zero and one for ValueError returning not a number, the same three calls give 5.0, zero and not a number. The tutorial notes that a try statement may have more than one except clause and at most one handler will be executed (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Brackets are still required with the as clause. In Python 3.14 the line except ZeroDivisionError, ValueError as e: is a syntax error with the message multiple exception types must be parenthesized when using 'as'. PEP 758 also warns that in Python 2 the unparenthesized form meant something else, with the first name as the exception type and the second as the variable that receives the exception. The new form does not reintroduce that meaning (Galindo Salgado and Cannon, 2024). A program that must run on a release before 3.14 should keep the brackets. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Exception object
slides.say: Catching an error is often not enough, since the program or its user also wants to know what went wrong. The object carries that information: its type says what kind of failure it was, and its arguments hold the details, usually a message in words. A program can print the message, write it to a file or look at its parts, which the textbook's examples do not do. For try: 1 / 0 followed by except ZeroDivisionError as e:, the type's name is ZeroDivisionError, the text of e is division by zero, and e.args is ('division by zero',), a tuple, which is a fixed group of values written in brackets. The same pattern with int('puppy') gives a ValueError whose text is invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'puppy'. The tutorial notes that built-in exception types define __str__() to print all the arguments without explicitly accessing .args (Python Software Foundation, 2026). That is why print(e) shows the message alone. The library reference describes args as the tuple of arguments given when the exception object is created, and says that some built-in exceptions expect a certain number of arguments while others are usually called only with a single string giving an error message (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The name after as does not survive the except clause. The reference says that when an exception has been assigned using as target, it is cleared at the end of the except clause, so the exception must be assigned to a different name to be able to refer to it after the clause (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program that prints e after the clause fails with NameError: name 'e' is not defined, while a program that first stores e in another name, as in saved = e, can still read saved.args.

slides.title: Traceback
slides.say: The traceback is the first tool for finding a bug, because it says both what failed and where. The textbook uses it in just this way: from the line number given in the error message, you know that the return statement in spam() is causing the error (Sweigart, 2025). Reading it from the bottom up, first the message and then the lines above it, is quicker than reading the program from the top. For the textbook's zeroDivide.py, the traceback has a first line, Traceback (most recent call last):, then one pair of lines for each call the error passed through, and last the line ZeroDivisionError: division by zero. Run as a program, the two calls it lists are the call print(spam(0)) at line 6 of the main program and the statement return 42 / divide_by at line 2 inside spam. The traceback is the call stack written out. The call that was running when the error happened comes last, which is what the words most recent call last refer to. Each pair of lines names a file, a line number and the function in which the line sits, followed by the source line. The main program is shown as <module>. A program that ends this way also ends with exit status 1, the number that a program hands to the system when it ends, where zero means success. The printed form is not identical between releases. The textbook's listing shows a Windows path, and your own file names will differ. The tutorial's examples also show marker lines under the source line, which the textbook's listing does not have, and the wording of some messages changed between 3.12 and 3.14, so a program should not compare the text of a traceback.

slides.title: ZeroDivisionError
slides.say: Division by zero has no answer, so the language cannot return a value, and the only honest choices are to stop or to hand the decision to the program. Making it an exception that can be caught lets the code that knows the meaning of the division decide what to do, as the chapter's function spam does with a message. The chapter's function returns 42 / divide_by. Called with 2 it gives 21.0 and with 12 it gives 3.5, and with 0 it raises ZeroDivisionError: division by zero. The statements 1 // 0 and 1 % 0 raise the same exception, because floor division and modulo also have a second operand that must not be zero. The check is made when the operation runs, not when the program is read, so a program that contains 42 / 0 starts normally and fails only when that line is reached. The exception object is created, the statement stops and the search for a handler begins, as for every exception. ZeroDivisionError is a subclass of ArithmeticError, so a handler written for ArithmeticError would catch it too. The wording of the message depends on the release. In Python 3.14 the statements 1 / 0, 1 // 0 and 1 % 0 all end with division by zero. In Python 3.12 the same statements end with division by zero, integer division or modulo by zero, and integer modulo by zero. A program should catch the type of the exception, which is stable, and should not compare the text. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Exception hierarchy
slides.say: The tree decides which handler catches which error. The tutorial states the rule: a class in an except clause matches exceptions which are instances of the class itself or one of its derived classes, but not the other way around, so an except clause listing a derived class does not match instances of its base classes (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A programmer can therefore choose how wide a handler is, from one exact error to a whole family. In the chapter, UnboundLocalError is a subclass of NameError and RecursionError is a subclass of RuntimeError, which is why a handler for NameError also catches a local variable used too early. A program that divides by zero inside try, and has except ArithmeticError, prints the type ZeroDivisionError for what it caught. A handler for KeyError does not catch it, and the error passes to the outer handler. When an exception is raised, Python goes through the except clauses of the try statement from top to bottom, and the first matching clause is triggered (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A narrow class must therefore be written before a broad one, because a broad class written first matches everything below it. If a clause for ArithmeticError is written before a clause for ZeroDivisionError, the narrow clause never runs, because dividing by zero is already handled by the first. The tutorial shows the same effect with three classes: listed from the base class first, its example prints B three times instead of B, C, D. Not every exception is under Exception. KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit are direct subclasses of BaseException, and the reference gives the reason: they inherit from BaseException so as not to be accidentally caught by code that catches Exception and thus prevent the interpreter from exiting (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A handler written for Exception is therefore the widest handler that is normally safe. The widest of all, for BaseException, would also stop a user from pressing Ctrl-C to end the program. slides.title: Short programs
slides.say: This branch collects the programs that the chapter uses to put its ideas to work. Two of them are short animation programs, zigzag and spike, which print lines of characters until the user stops them. Two are practice programs, the Collatz sequence and input validation, which the textbook leaves to the reader. Each program is built from parts that have already been explained: functions, loops, string replication, try and except. The textbook introduces the first program with the words that it will use the programming concepts you have learned so far to create a small animation program (Sweigart, 2025). Writing a whole program is the real test of understanding, because it shows whether the pieces fit together, which a single statement cannot show. The programs also bring in three small tools that the chapter has not met yet, the time.sleep function, the KeyboardInterrupt exception and the sys.exit function. The branch has two groups. Animation covers zigzag and spike and the three tools they need. Practice programs covers the Collatz sequence and the extra step of making that program safe against wrong input. Every program here has the same shape: an import line, a block of work that may repeat, and a try statement whose except clause deals with the one event that the program expects, the user pressing Ctrl-C. Reading them as variations of that shape makes each one shorter to understand. The animation programs never end by themselves, so they cannot be run to completion in a test. The numbers quoted in this branch come from the same logic executed for a fixed number of steps, without the pause, and are labelled as such. This divider is the branch's own description from the chapter corpus; the boxes under it name every concept in the branch, so the room can see how far there is to go.

slides.title: Animation programs
slides.say: An animation program draws something new at regular intervals, so that the output seems to move. The textbook's two examples need no graphics: each prints a line of characters, waits one tenth of a second and prints the next, and the changing position or length of the lines makes a pattern that scrolls up the screen (Sweigart, 2025). These programs show a loop that does not stop, and the problem that follows from it: a program that never ends needs a way for the user to end it. The solution the textbook gives is the same in both programs, and it is the reason that this group also contains the sections on waiting, on interruption and on exiting. The sections follow the order of the textbook: the zigzag program, the spike program, the time.sleep function both programs use for their pause, the KeyboardInterrupt exception that Ctrl-C raises, and the sys.exit function that the exception handler calls. Use this slide to say what the next few slides are for before any of them appears: the table on the right is exactly the concepts that follow, each with the example the chapter uses for it. Click the rows in one at a time if the room is new to the material.

slides.title: Zigzag program
slides.say: The program shows how a few lines of state can produce a changing picture. Nothing in it is complicated, but it uses a main loop, a decision that changes direction at two limits, and string replication in one place, which makes it a good first program that combines the tools of the earlier chapters. The first three lines it prints are the eight asterisks with no indent, one space and two spaces. The main loop is while True. In each pass print(' ' * indent, end='') prints the spaces and, because end is an empty string, no newline, and then a second print prints the asterisks. If indent_increasing is true, indent grows by 1, and when it reaches 20 the flag is set to false; otherwise indent shrinks by 1, and when it reaches 0 the flag is set to true. Executed for 41 passes without the pause, and numbering the passes from 0, the indent is 0 in pass 0, 1 in pass 1, 19 in pass 19, 20 in pass 20, 19 in pass 21, 1 in pass 39 and 0 in pass 40. The largest value is 20, so one trip there and back takes 40 passes. The program is wrapped in a try statement so that Ctrl-C can end it, which the sections on KeyboardInterrupt and sys.exit explain. Without the wrapper, the same keypress would end the program with a traceback. The upper limit, 20, is written into the program as a plain number, so changing how far the band travels means changing that number in the test.

slides.title: Spike program
slides.say: It is a short example of how the range function controls a loop. The two loops differ only in their range, and each print uses the same expression, '-' * (i * i), so the shape of the whole picture is decided by two lines of numbers. The first loop uses range(1, 9), which gives 1 through 8, and the second uses range(7, 1, -1), which gives 7 down to 2. The lengths of the printed lines are therefore 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 49, 36, 25, 16, 9 and 4, which is fourteen lines for each trip through the main loop. In each pass of a loop the variable i takes the next value from its range, and the string '-' is replicated i * i times. The textbook points out that the range of the second loop starts at 7, so the longest line, 64, is printed once, and that it counts down to 1, not including 1, so the shortest line of the second half is 4. The textbook also says that you can modify the 9 and the 7 values if you want to change how wide the spike becomes (Sweigart, 2025). The textbook calls the lengths exponentially longer, but squares grow more slowly than that. The differences between neighbouring lengths in the first half are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15, which grow by a steady 2, a pattern of quadratic growth. Each trip through the main loop prints 8 lines from the first range and 6 from the second.

slides.title: The time.sleep function
slides.say: Without a pause, a program that prints a line in every pass of a loop would run so fast that the whole animation would fly past in an instant. A short pause gives the eye time to follow the pattern. The function is also used wherever a program has to wait, for example between attempts to reach something that is not ready. Both animation programs call time.sleep(0.1) in every pass of their main loop, after the print call. The function belongs to the time module, so the program needs the line import time first, and the call is written with the module name in front, like the other module functions of this chapter. The call returns None, as print does, and it returns after the pause. A program that measures the time with time.perf_counter() around time.sleep(0.1) finds that at least a tenth of a second passed and, on an ordinary run, well under a second. The reference says that perf_counter includes time elapsed during sleep (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The pause is not exact. The reference says that the suspension time may be longer than requested by an arbitrary amount, because of the scheduling of other activity in the system (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program should not use the pause as a clock. The pause also does not block Ctrl-C: when an interrupt arrives during a five second sleep, the sleep ends early with KeyboardInterrupt, and in the check the program ended in under three seconds. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: KeyboardInterrupt
slides.say: A program that never ends by itself needs a way out. The user can always end it with the interrupt key, but if the exception is not caught, the textbook says the program crashes with an ugly error message (Sweigart, 2025). Catching it lets the program stop in the way the programmer chooses. In the zigzag and spike programs, the whole loop is inside a try clause, and the except clause at the end names KeyboardInterrupt and calls sys.exit(). When an interrupt arrives while the program sleeps, the handler runs and prints its message. The check in this corpus starts a second program that is sleeping, sends it the interrupt and observes that its handler ran. The reference notes that during execution, a check for interrupts is made regularly (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Where the interrupt is noticed, it is raised like any other exception, so it travels outwards through the frames until a handler for KeyboardInterrupt is found. The animation programs put the try statement outside the loop, so the handler is found no matter in which pass the key was pressed. KeyboardInterrupt is not an Exception. The reference says that it inherits from BaseException so as to not be accidentally caught by code that catches Exception and thus prevent the interpreter from exiting (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A handler written as except Exception does not catch the interrupt, and the interrupt passes on to an outer KeyboardInterrupt handler. A handler for BaseException would catch it, which is why that class is the wrong target for a handler meant for ordinary errors.

slides.title: The sys.exit function
slides.say: A program needs a deliberate way to finish from the middle of its code, for instance when it has detected a problem or when the user asks to stop. The optional argument tells the operating system and other programs whether the run succeeded, which matters as soon as a program is started by another one. Called with no argument, sys.exit() ends the program with exit status 0, which the reference calls successful termination. Called with an integer such as 2, the status is 2, and any nonzero value is considered abnormal termination. Called with a string, as in sys.exit('bye'), the string is printed to the error stream, the channel on which error messages are written, and the exit status is 1. The reference calls the last form a quick way to exit a program when an error occurs (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Since the function only raises an exception, the program does not end at once: the exception travels outwards like any other. The reference says that cleanup actions specified by finally clauses of try statements are honored, and that it is possible to intercept the exit attempt at an outer level (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A handler for SystemExit can read the status from the code attribute of the exception, which is None when no argument was given, and the program then keeps running. A handler for Exception does not intercept the exit, because SystemExit inherits from BaseException so that it is not accidentally caught by code that catches Exception (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The reverse mistake is easy too: a program that catches SystemExit and does nothing with it will not end, which is what the reference means by intercepting the exit attempt. slides.title: Practice programs
slides.say: The textbook ends the chapter with practice programs: tasks for the reader to write without a model solution (Sweigart, 2025). The two tasks in this chapter build on one another. The first asks for a function named collatz and a program that calls it, and the second adds try and except statements to that program. Practice programs turn the chapter's concepts into habits. The first needs a function with a parameter and a return value, the second needs error handling around user input, so between them they use almost every idea of the chapter. The sections of this group present the two tasks, say what each one needs from the chapter, and point out where the textbook's wording needs a correction or a limit that the reader would otherwise find the hard way. slides.title: Collatz sequence
slides.say: It practises the main ideas of the chapter in a few lines: a parameter, a return value that is used in the next call, and a loop that stops on a condition. It is also a famous problem. The textbook calls it the simplest impossible math problem, and says that even mathematicians are not sure why the sequence reaches 1 (Sweigart, 2025). Starting at 3, the program prints 3 10 5 16 8 4 2 1, as in the textbook's sample, and the rule used is the same on every step: 3 is odd, so the next value is 3 * 3 + 1, which is 10; 10 is even, so the next is 5. Counting the steps, the start 3 reaches 1 in 7 steps and its largest value is 16, while the start 27 needs 111 steps and reaches 9232 on the way. A number is even if number % 2 == 0, which is the hint the textbook gives. The program stores the returned value back in the same variable, n = collatz(n), and the loop condition is n != 1. To print all the values on one line, the print calls need the named parameter end=' ' so that a space replaces the newline. The textbook's hint names sep=' ' for this, but sep only changes what goes between several values in one call, and with a single value in each call it changes nothing: printing 3 and then 10 with sep=' ' still gives two lines. The textbook says that the sequence works for any integer, but the loop does not end for all of them. For 0 the rule gives 0 // 2, which is 0 again, and for -1 it gives -2 and then -1 again, so after 1000 steps the values are still 0 and -1 and a program that waits for 1 would never finish. The sequence is a question about positive integers. Input from the user should therefore also be checked for being greater than zero, not only for being a number. slides.title: Input validation
slides.say: The user is the least predictable part of a program. The program of the previous section works when the user types a number and ends with a traceback when the user types a word. A handler around the conversion turns that traceback into a message the user can act on, and a program can then ask again. For int('puppy') the handler receives a ValueError whose text is invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'puppy'. In the textbook's wording, the except clause then prints a message to the user saying they must enter an integer. A small function can wrap the idea: to_int returns int(text) inside a try clause, prints You must enter an integer. in the except clause for ValueError, and so returns 42 for '42' and None for 'puppy'. Only the line that does the conversion belongs in the try clause, and the exception type to name is the one that int raises. The None from the failed conversion is the value Python supplies when a function ends without a return statement, which means the code that uses the result must be ready for it. The handler catches only ValueError. A user who just presses Enter gives int an empty string, which is also a ValueError, but a value of another type, such as None passed by mistake, would raise a TypeError and the program would still crash. Also, as the previous section noted, an integer is not always a valid input: 0 and negative integers pass the conversion and still never reach 1 in the sequence. slides.title: Modern practice
slides.say: Modern practice is the part of the chapter that goes beyond the textbook's list of topics to what a programmer needs around functions today. It has two groups. The first, Annotations, is about the notes that can be written on a function's parameters and result, and about the way Python 3.14 stores them. The second, Style, is about the habits that make a function easy to use and to read: treating it as a black box, naming it well and commenting it. An advanced course reads code written by other people, and that code uses all of these. Annotations appear in the signature of almost every function in a modern library, and the change in Python 3.14 decides whether code that uses them runs at all on a given release. Style is not decoration: the black box idea is the reason that functions are useful, and PEP 8 is the style guide for the code of Python's standard library (Van Rossum et al., 2001). A function from a current library may look like def add(a: int, b: int = 0) -> int:, with a note after each parameter and one after the arrow. The same function is used by its callers without reading its body, is named in lowercase words joined by underscores, and has comments only where the code needs them. The sections follow the order in which a reader meets the ideas: first what an annotation is and what Python does with it, then the 3.14 change that postpones the evaluation, then the three style topics. Each section marks the release in which its behaviour holds. Annotations are the area where releases differ most, since the behaviour of a definition with an undefined name in its annotation changed between Python 3.12 and 3.14. The sections state the release for every claim. This divider is the branch's own description from the chapter corpus; the boxes under it name every concept in the branch, so the room can see how far there is to go.

slides.title: Annotations
slides.say: An annotation is an expression written next to a parameter or after the arrow that follows the parameter list. PEP 3107 defines function annotations, both for parameters and return values, as completely optional and as nothing more than a way of associating arbitrary Python expressions with various parts of a function at compile-time (Winter and Lownds, 2006). The usual expression is the name of a type, such as int. A note on what a function expects and gives back is information for the reader, for the editor and for tools that check programs, and it needs no comment to keep it in step with the code. Python 3.14 changes when the notes are evaluated, which is why this group has two sections: the notation itself and its newest behaviour. The first section describes the notation and what Python does with it, which is almost nothing. The second describes deferred evaluation, adopted in Python 3.14, under which a note may name something that does not exist yet. Use this slide to say what the next few slides are for before any of them appears: the table on the right is exactly the concepts that follow, each with the example the chapter uses for it. Click the rows in one at a time if the room is new to the material.

slides.title: Function annotation
slides.say: Annotations let a function state its contract in its own signature. A reader sees at once that add expects two integers and gives back an integer, without opening the body. Editors and checking programs can use the same notes to warn about a call that does not fit. For def add(a: int, b: int = 0) -> int: return a + b, Python stores the notes and add.__annotations__ shows that a, b and the result are all marked with the type int. Calling add(2, 3) gives 5. Calling add('x', 'y') also works and gives 'xy', although the notes say int. PEP 3107 states that, by itself, Python does not attach any particular meaning or significance to annotations; it simply makes the expressions available in the function's __annotations__ attribute, and the only way that annotations take on meaning is when they are interpreted by third-party libraries (Winter and Lownds, 2006). The attribute pairs each parameter name with its note, and the note for the result is stored under the name return. In Python 3.12 all annotation expressions were evaluated when the function definition was executed, just like default values. A note is not a check. The call add('x', 'y') above shows that Python runs the function whatever the notes say. A lambda expression cannot carry annotations, which the language reference states and the lambda section of this chapter shows. And since the notes are real expressions, a wrong or misspelled name inside one is a real error in Python 3.12, which is the problem the next section addresses.

slides.title: Deferred annotations
slides.say: Before the change, a note that named something defined later in the file had to be written as a string, so that its evaluation would not fail. What's New says that it is no longer necessary to enclose annotations in strings if they contain forward references (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The change also lowers the cost of defining a function, since its notes are not evaluated until they are wanted. The line def f(x: Undefined) -> Missing: return x defines a function with two names that do not exist. Under Python 3.12 the definition itself fails with NameError: name 'Undefined' is not defined. Under Python 3.14 the definition succeeds, and f(3) returns 3. Asking for f.__annotations__ then raises the NameError, because that is the moment when the names are evaluated. The standard library module annotationlib reads the notes in one of three formats. The VALUE format evaluates them, as earlier releases did and fails on an undefined name; the FORWARDREF format replaces undefined names with special markers; and the STRING format returns the annotations as strings (Python Software Foundation, 2026). For the function above, the FORWARDREF format gives entries for x and the result without raising an error, and the STRING format gives the text Undefined for x and Missing for the result. Under Python 3.12 the module annotationlib does not exist. The change is a reason to read the release notes before moving a program between versions. slides.title: Style
slides.say: Style means the habits of writing and using a function that go beyond making it work. The textbook has one such idea, the black box, and PEP 8 is the style guide for the code in Python's standard library (Van Rossum et al., 2001). This group treats three habits: using a function without reading it, naming it and commenting it. How a function is meant to be used matters as much as how it is written. A program is read many more times than it is written, and each habit reduces the amount that a reader has to hold in mind: the black box lets the reader skip the body, a good name tells what the function does, and a good comment explains what the code cannot say. The three sections apply to the same small functions that the chapter has used: a function that doubles a number, a function that divides, a function that prints a greeting. Each states the rule of the style guide or the textbook that supports it, and shows what happens when the rule is broken. Use this slide to say what the next few slides are for before any of them appears: the table on the right is exactly the concepts that follow, each with the example the chapter uses for it. Click the rows in one at a time if the room is new to the material.

slides.title: Function as a black box
slides.say: The idea is what makes large programs possible. The textbook calls it fundamental to modern programming, because later chapters show modules with functions written by other people, which can be used without knowing how they work (Sweigart, 2025). A reader who may rely on a function's inputs and output only has far less to understand than one who must follow every line. In the program x = 1, then def f(): x = 99 and return x * 2, then print(f(), x), the function returns 198 and the global x is still 1. The assignment inside f created a local variable and left the global one alone, so nothing outside f can tell how f got its result. The idea rests on the scope rules of this chapter. Variables assigned in a function are local, so they disappear when the call ends, and a function that has no global statement cannot change a global variable. What goes in is the arguments, and what comes out is the return value. The textbook adds that because writing functions without global variables is encouraged, you usually do not have to worry about the function's code interacting with the rest of your program (Sweigart, 2025). The box is only as sealed as its author made it. A function that uses a global statement, or that reads a global variable that others may change, depends on something that is not in its parameters, and then the call f(2) no longer says everything about what the result will be. Printing instead of returning is the other leak: the output reaches a person but cannot be used by the caller.

slides.title: Function naming
slides.say: A function is called many more times than it is defined, so its name is what most readers see. A name that says what the function does lets a reader follow a program without opening the functions, which is the black box idea in practice. A common convention also lets a reader guess the name of a function, without looking it up. Python tells names apart by case. If the program defines Hello and then calls hello(), the call fails with NameError: name 'hello' is not defined, since no function with that exact name exists. A name that is a reserved keyword is rejected before the program runs: the line def = 3 gives SyntaxError: invalid syntax. PEP 8 also covers the case in which the best name is a keyword. If a function argument's name clashes with a reserved keyword, it is generally better to append a single trailing underscore rather than use an abbreviation or spelling corruption, so class_ is better than clss (Van Rossum et al., 2001). The check keyword.iskeyword tells whether a name is reserved: it says yes for def and for None and for lambda, and no for print, which is an ordinary function. The guide is a convention, not a rule enforced by Python: a function named Hello works exactly as well as one named hello, provided the calls use the same spelling. PEP 8 also warns that the guide is about consistency, and has a section titled A Foolish Consistency is the Hobgoblin of Little Minds, which says that in some cases the guide does not apply. The guide itself says that consistency within a project is more important than consistency with the guide (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

slides.title: Comment
slides.say: Code says what it does; a comment can say why. The textbook's examples use comments in this way, such as the one inside the try clause that tells the reader that any code in the block that causes ZeroDivisionError will not crash the program (Sweigart, 2025). PEP 8 adds a warning about the cost: comments that contradict the code are worse than no comments, and keeping them up to date when the code changes is a priority (Van Rossum et al., 2001). In the line print('# not a comment')  # this is a comment, the first hash is inside quotes and is part of the text, and the second one starts a comment. The program prints # not a comment. A line that starts with # is skipped completely, so a statement placed behind a hash, such as # print('hidden'), does not run. PEP 8 distinguishes two kinds. Block comments generally apply to some or all of the code that follows them and are indented to the same level as that code; each line starts with a # and a single space. Inline comments are on the same line as a statement, are separated from it by at least two spaces, and should be used sparingly (Van Rossum et al., 2001). Comments should be complete sentences. A comment that restates the code adds noise. PEP 8 gives the example x = x + 1 with the comment Increment x, and calls such comments unnecessary and in fact distracting, whereas a comment such as Compensate for border is useful (Van Rossum et al., 2001). A hash inside a string literal does not start a comment, which is the mistake the example above demonstrates.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.say: 1. What is the main idea of a function in this chapter? The answer is: A named block of code that can be run from many places, take values in and hand a value back The chapter gives a block of code a name so it can be run from many places, with values passed in and a value coming out. 2. Which keyword begins the statement that creates a new function? The answer is: def Creating Functions introduces the def statement, which is followed by a call that runs the function. 3. When does the body of a function run? The answer is: Each time the function is called, and not when the def statement is executed A def statement only creates the function and binds its name; the indented body executes when the function is called. 4. What does a function call evaluate to? The answer is: Its return value, so the call can be used wherever a value can Return values describe what a call evaluates to, which lets a call stand in for a value. 5. What does this program print? The answer is: 12 The inner call returns 6 and that value is the argument of the outer call, which returns 12. Let the room answer before each click. The full bank of 142 questions for this chapter, with a reason for every wrong option, is on the chapter page.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.say: 6. What does a return statement with no expression after it give back? The answer is: None If an expression list is present it is evaluated, else None is substituted, and control leaves the function. 7. Which question does the call stack answer? The answer is: Where execution goes back to when a function returns The Call Stack explains where execution goes when a function returns. 8. Why does Python remember the line that made a call? The answer is: So that execution can return there when the function ends Python remembers the line that called the function, so the call does not send execution one way to the top of the body. 9. Where are frame objects added to and removed from the call stack? The answer is: Only at the top Frame objects are added to and removed from the top of the call stack only, and the top frame is the function currently running. 10. Which question do the scope topics answer? The answer is: Which variable a name refers to Local and global scopes, the scope rules and the global statement say which variable a name refers to. Let the room answer before each click. The full bank of 142 questions for this chapter, with a reason for every wrong option, is on the chapter page.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.say: 11. When is the scope of a function created and destroyed? The answer is: Created when the function is called and destroyed when it returns Scopes are containers created when a program starts or a function is called; a function's local scope is destroyed when the call returns. 12. What happens to a variable assigned inside a function when the function returns? The answer is: It is destroyed with the local scope of that call A variable assigned inside a function exists in that call's local scope, which is destroyed when the function returns. 13. What does exception handling change about an error in a program? The answer is: It turns a crash into something the program can recover from Exception handling turns an error from a crash into something a program can recover from. 14. Which statements decide what happens after an error raises an exception? The answer is: try and except An error raises an exception, and try and except statements decide what happens next. 15. What happens to the rest of a try clause after one of its lines raises a matching exception? The answer is: It is skipped, the except clause runs, and execution continues after the try statement When an exception occurs the rest of the try clause is skipped and, if the type matches, the except clause runs. Let the room answer before each click. The full bank of 142 questions for this chapter, with a reason for every wrong option, is on the chapter page.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.say: 16. Which tools do the chapter's short programs bring in that the chapter had not covered yet? The answer is: time.sleep, KeyboardInterrupt and sys.exit The animation programs pause with time.sleep and stop on Ctrl-C by catching KeyboardInterrupt and calling sys.exit. 17. Why do the zigzag and spike programs put their loop inside a try statement? The answer is: So that Ctrl-C can end the endless loop without an ugly error The loop never ends by itself, and the except clause for KeyboardInterrupt calls sys.exit to stop it cleanly. 18. What does the variable indent_increasing decide in the zigzag program? The answer is: Whether indent grows or shrinks on the next pass of the loop It is True while the band moves right and is switched when indent reaches 20 or 0. 19. What is the point of the modern-practice topics next to the chapter's functions? The answer is: They add what current Python offers around functions An advanced course pairs the chapter's functions with what current Python adds around them. 20. Which function header carries annotations on a parameter and on the result? The answer is: def area(w: int, h: int) -> int: Annotations on a function's parameters and result are written with a colon after a parameter and an arrow before the final colon. Let the room answer before each click. The full bank of 142 questions for this chapter, with a reason for every wrong option, is on the chapter page.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.say: 21. What does Python do with the annotation int in def f(a: int)? The answer is: Stores it with the function but does not check the arguments against it Annotations are kept in the function's __annotations__ and have no effect on the call unless a tool reads them.
